Key Finding: The 2023 National Readership Survey reported that only 42% of Filipino adults and 47% of children read non-school books, with limited access to books the primary reason for decline.
APA Reference: Philippine Information Agency. (2024, March 22). Pay more attention to reading, literacy NBDB urges. https://pia.gov.ph/news/pay-more-attention-to-reading-literacy-nbdb-urges-works-to-get-more-filipinos-to-read/

Key Finding: The 2023 survey found book availability was the primary consideration when Filipinos selected non-school books, and printed books were preferred by both adults and children.
APA Reference: Philippine Information Agency. (2024, March 22). Pay more attention to reading, literacy NBDB urges. https://pia.gov.ph/news/pay-more-attention-to-reading-literacy-nbdb-urges-works-to-get-more-filipinos-to-read/

Key Finding: Learning poverty remains severe in the Philippines, with 91% of late-primary-age children unable to read and understand an age-appropriate text.
APA Reference: World Bank. (2024). Philippines learning poverty brief. https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/099090524085540633/pdf/P179209-b0057b3a-fd8c-476a-a1c6-271b276117ff.pdf

Key Finding: Only 56.1% of Philippine households had internet access in 2020, with access below 50% in Visayas and Mindanao, creating a nationwide reach constraint.
APA Reference: Asian Development Bank. (2024). Philippines: Country partnership strategy 2024–2029. https://www.adb.org/sites/default/files/linked-documents/cps-phi-2024-2029-isga.pdf

Key Finding: Internet use in the Philippines rose from 25% to 75% between 2010 and 2022, but connectivity benefits were stronger in urban than rural areas.
APA Reference: Asian Development Bank. (2025). Mobile internet connectivity and household wealth in the Philippines. https://seads.adb.org/publication/mobile-internet-connectivity-and-household-wealth-philippines

Key Finding: UNESCO reports that affordable, reliable broadband and basic ICT skills remain uneven in the Philippines, limiting inclusive participation in digital services.
APA Reference: UNESCO. (2025). UNESCO AI readiness assessment report: Anchoring ethics in AI governance in the Philippines. https://philippines.un.org/en/306159-unesco-ai-readiness-assessment-report-anchoring-ethics-ai-governance-philippines

Key Finding: The NBDB identified limited access and affordability as barriers to reading and called for policies that enable publishers to provide more affordable books.
APA Reference: Philippine Information Agency. (2024, March 22). Pay more attention to reading, literacy NBDB urges. https://pia.gov.ph/news/pay-more-attention-to-reading-literacy-nbdb-urges-works-to-get-more-filipinos-to-read/

Key Finding: Mobile internet connectivity is associated with higher household wealth in the Philippines, with effects that persist across education levels.
APA Reference: Asian Development Bank. (2025). Mobile internet connectivity. https://seads.adb.org/publication/mobile-internet-connectivity-and-household-wealth-philippines

Key Finding: One in four Filipinos remains vulnerable to poverty, making free or low-cost access to books economically relevant for many households.
APA Reference: World Bank. (2026). Building the Filipino middle class. https://www.worldbank.org/en/country/philippines/publication/key-findings-building-the-filipino-middle-class-towards-resilient-futures-and-poverty-eradication

Key Finding: Life-cycle analysis found that paper-book impacts are concentrated upstream in paper procurement, while unsold books add burdens through production, delivery, and recycling.
APA Reference: Shimizu, H., & Nagata, K. (2010). Comparison of life-cycle CO2 emissions for paper-based and electronic books. https://doi.org/10.11413/nig.47.089

Key Finding: UNEP identifies reuse as a core circular-economy shift that can reduce damage to human health, the environment, and the climate.
APA Reference: United Nations Environment Programme. (2023). Turning off the tap: How the world can end plastic pollution and create a circular economy. https://wedocs.unep.org/20.500.11822/44842

Key Finding: Philippine solid-waste policy requires barangays or clusters of barangays to establish recovery facilities for segregation and recycling.
APA Reference: Department of Environment and Natural Resources. (n.d.). Handbook on ecological solid waste management. https://faspselib.denr.gov.ph/Materials/Detail/66452379-bf37-4bf6-9682-e4b981aebfa5

Key Finding: The Philippine Creative Industries Development Act includes publishing and printed media in national creative-industry planning and promotes market development and partnerships.
APA Reference: Republic Act No. 11904, Philippine Creative Industries Development Act (2022). https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra2022/ra_11904_2022.html

Key Finding: The National Alliance of Reading Advocates agenda calls for nationwide reading communities, engagement opportunities, and support for Filipino content through books.
APA Reference: National Alliance of Reading Advocates. (2025). Agenda 2025–2030. https://books.gov.ph/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/National-Alliance-of-Reading-Advocates-Agenda-2025-2030-1.pdf

Key Finding: The Philippine government and World Bank are prioritizing nationwide foundational-literacy support and improved access to inclusive learning materials.
APA Reference: World Bank. (2026). World Bank backs better learning for 21 million Filipino students. https://www.worldbank.org/en/news/press-release/2026/04/03/world-bank-backs-better-learning-for-21-million-filipino-students

Key Finding: The Philippine Data Privacy Act protects privacy and communication while requiring personal information in systems to be secured and protected.
APA Reference: Republic Act No. 10173, Data Privacy Act of 2012 (2012). https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra2012/ra_10173_2012.html

Key Finding: The Data Privacy Act implementing rules require transparency, legitimate purpose, proportionality, data minimization, security, and retention limits.
APA Reference: National Privacy Commission. (2016). Implementing rules and regulations of the Data Privacy Act of 2012. https://privacy.gov.ph/implementing-rules%20regulations-data-privacy-act-2012/

Key Finding: National Privacy Commission guidance requires privacy-by-design, privacy-by-default, lawful basis, proportionality, retention limits, and privacy impact assessment across system lifecycles.
APA Reference: National Privacy Commission. (2025). Advisory 2025-02: Privacy by design and default. https://privacy.gov.ph/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/FINAL_NPC_Advisory2025-02.pdf

Key Finding: UNESCO’s AI ethics framework emphasizes proportionality, privacy, transparency, human oversight, fairness, non-discrimination, and sustainability for digital systems.
APA Reference: UNESCO. (2021). Recommendation on the ethics of artificial intelligence. https://www.unesco.org/en/legal-affairs/recommendation-ethics-artificial-intelligence

Key Finding: UNESCO warns that digital systems can deepen inequality and digital divides unless access is inclusive across language, culture, age, disability, and vulnerable groups.
APA Reference: UNESCO. (2021). Recommendation on the ethics of artificial intelligence. https://www.unesco.org/en/legal-affairs/recommendation-ethics-artificial-intelligence

Key Finding: OECD reports that online safety risks threaten user well-being and trust, while countries increasingly require platforms to improve safety rather than rely only on self-regulation.
APA Reference: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development. (n.d.). Online safety and well-being. https://www.oecd.org/en/topics/policy-issues/online-safety-and-well-being.html
